title: Dance hall customs: eating at midnight, sitting down, repertoire
summary: Howard describes how bands called players together, took a free supper at midnight, sat instead of standing, and played waltzes, blues and popular numbers.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I see. Is it that they were practicing sort of? Well, no.
It just, well, no. At that time, they didn't have a union and stuff like that. The fellas might be scattered around in a wholesome place. He called them. He was calling them.

He was calling them. Yeah, that's what, that's what. So maybe it was sort of like these warming up, you know, or- No, no. You also just had so much music in him, he had to keep playing all the time. No, no.

No, no. It would get the fellas together. I got them together. See? And I mean, like you play a number, you play like that, and that guy play a number two, then everybody take a walk. Of course you had to go from eight to two or something like that. It was long hours, but, and then at that time, when I come, I come along in the, in the, in the, in the kind of, uh, last part of the thing, but, uh, the, uh, at 12 o'clock, you come off the stand, everybody, and sit at a table long under this, and have something to eat. I don't make no sandwich.
Mm-hmm. It's like regular, uh, big balls, like- Big balls, kind of, all of them places.
You come down, and everybody eat, and drink. That's for free. At 12 o'clock.
12 o'clock.

You come down and eat, and we still have those bunkies on Monday. That's plenty of, all that playing like the fellas playing now, and I don't know where they get that stuff but standing up for the Dixieland. You get to sit down. Everybody sit down.
Everybody sit down.
You stand up if you're going to take a solo or something. Mm-hmm. I think that's true.
There wasn't no standing up proposition.
But I know, what I'm talking about, they're representing the Dixieland business and the, that, that old time jazz, but there wasn't nobody standing up.
No, that's-

I don't understand that book. Burst, Burban Street, isn't it? It must be. But there wasn't no such thing. When we went to New York to play at Charles Brammer, that they want to put seats up there first. I said no. Joyce said no, standing. I said, well, God, a boy, you, all of them, this is not.
I don't know how to do it. You can relax more except for families, right? I know you can. You see.
But that, that's the way, that's the way it is now. You have to keep it going that way.

Well, in those old days, like at the economy hall, there are different halls, did they play more blues after midnight, I've heard, than the old days they did sometimes? They saved most of their blues until late at night?

Well, they saved more of the blues until people get crowded in there. And then you worked it like that. You could work it easier. And I mean it's like out there, they didn't play Panama all night long with all that fancy music. They played waltz, blues, popular numbers would come out, they played all that. But the majority of the people, now they guys are kind of funny, they think you got to just play Panama and Tagore. That ain't that, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, that ain't, not the way I, the part I know of it. You play a new number, like all the nice numbers come out, who's never could read the band, they go buy the music, and they play it until other guys get on to the number, and play a new number too.
That's right.
I mean, that's, when I was a kid, that's the way it was. But now, if you don't sit there and play when the sins go marching all night long, you ain't nowhere.
